integrated_description: Publication is presumed against unless provenance and lawful usability are established to a reasonable, actionable standard of confidence—unclear or demonstrably unlawful origin (e.g., hacking, coercion, unlawful surveillance) triggers non-publication of the document and its excerpts, with reporting limited strictly to independently corroborated, anonymized, high-level information only if a serious public-interest accountability test is met. Legal counsel's conclusion on lawful usability is treated as decisive, not merely advisory, and scope of publication is strictly limited to what is necessary for the public-interest purpose, with mandatory redaction of personal identifiers, intimate details, non-public conduct, surveillance context, and any information elevating harassment or safety risk. Seeking comment from affected parties remains a fairness obligation but does not resolve legal or provenance uncertainty, and verification of authenticity alone is explicitly insufficient to authorize publication.
integration_rationale: All three stakeholders converged on the same three structural tightening priorities—provenance-based presumption against publication, decisive legal review, and strict necessity-scoped redaction—making full integration achievable without trade-offs. The only nuance resolved was stakeholder_b's emphasis on avoiding amplification of privacy-violating leaks, which was incorporated as the prohibition on republishing the document or large excerpts when unlawful acquisition methods are evident.
